result:
Walking.

It is the most ancient form of travel, older than wheels, roads, language itself. Before we spoke, we walked. We crossed savannas, followed rivers, crested hills. Our bodies are built for it: the Achilles tendon, the arched foot, the gluteus maximus — all designed for endurance, for covering distance at a steady pace. Humans are not the fastest animals, but we are among the best at long-distance running and walking. A horse can outrun us in a sprint, but over twenty miles on a hot day, with a cool head and a steady stride, a human can walk a horse into the ground.

And yet, we have largely forgotten this. We sit. We ride. We scroll. Walking has become a leisure activity, an exercise video, a way to get from the parking lot to the store. We rarely walk because it is the only way. And when we do walk, we usually hurry — heads down, earbuds in, hurrying toward the next thing, as if walking itself were a delay, a cost, a thing to be minimized.

I want to argue for walking as a way of thinking, a way of being, a way of being in time. Not walking as exercise. Not walking as transport. Walking as ritual. Walking as prayer. Walking as reading.

There is a tradition here. Nietzsche walked — famously — through the hills of Sils Maria, and said that his philosophy was born on foot. "All truly great thoughts are conceived while walking," he wrote. Rousseau walked in the Alps and the Jura, writing his *Reveries of a Solitary Walker*, which is perhaps the greatest book ever written about walking, though it is really a book about thinking, about drifting, about letting the mind wander as the feet wander.

Wordsworth walked. Keats walked. Thoreau walked, and wrote an entire essay about it, arguing that walking is a kind of sauntering toward the holy land — that the word "saunter" comes from "sainte-terre," holy earth, or from "sans terre," without land, landless. A saunterer is one who does not own land, who is free. Blake walked through London. Dickens walked the city at night, thirty miles at a stretch, composing his novels in his head. The list goes on.

Why does walking generate thought? There is something about the rhythm. The steady cadence of footsteps — left, right, left, right — seems to entrain the brain, to calm the noisy chatter of the default mode network and allow deeper currents to surface. The body moves; the mind rests, or rather, the mind moves in a different way, less goal-directed, more associative. It is as if the thinking part of the brain hands the keys over to the wandering part. The problem you have been stuck on for hours suddenly opens up, not because you solved it, but because you stopped trying to solve it.

There is also the sheer input. When you walk, you see things. You notice the way light falls on a brick wall. The tilt of a mailbox. A dog tied to a fire hydrant, waiting patiently. The smell of rain on pavement. The sound of a distant train. These details — small, irrelevant, beautiful — feed the mind. They remind us that the world is bigger and stranger than our worries. They give us metaphors, images, analogies. A walk is a kind of collage.

I like to walk in the evening, just before dusk. The light changes. Everything softens. The streetlights begin to come on, one by one, in their staggered way, and the sky turns that deep, uncertain blue that is neither day nor night. People are coming home. The windows of houses glow amber. There is a feeling of suspension, of being between, of hovering at a threshold. It is the hour when secrets feel safe.

I walk without a destination, or with a destination that is just an excuse. I walk in loops. I walk the same streets over and over, and I have come to know them the way you know an old friend's face — the crack in the sidewalk, the oak tree that leans slightly to the left, the house with the blue door, the corner where the wind always picks up.

There is a particular corner in my neighborhood, a spot where two streets meet at an odd angle, and there is a low stone wall there. A few years ago, someone painted a tiny mural on the wall — a whale breaching, done in faded blues and greens. It is chipped and weather-beaten now, but every time I pass it, I look at it, and I think about the person who painted it, and the thousands of people who have walked past it since, and the fact that no one owns it, and that it will fade completely one day, and that is okay.

Walking is also a way of being with others, or of being alone in a way that is not lonely. You can walk with a friend and not talk, and it will not be awkward. You can walk with yourself and not be bored. You can walk in a city, surrounded by thousands of strangers, and feel a profound sense of kinship with them — all of us moving, all of us breathing, all of us headed somewhere, even if we don't know where.

In recent years, I have noticed that I walk less. I drive more. I sit more. My screen time is up; my step count is down. This is a loss. It is a loss of body, but also a loss of mind, a loss of the unstructured time that allows thoughts to develop, to cross-pollinate, to ripen.

There is a quote often attributed to Kierkegaard (though its origins are murky): "I have walked myself into my best thoughts." I believe this. I have experienced it. The hardest problems in my life were not solved at a desk. They were solved on foot, usually when I wasn't trying to solve them, sometimes in the middle of a long walk, when the answer simply arrived, unbidden, like a bird landing on a branch.

The poet William Butler Yeats wrote about "the fascination of what's difficult," and about how he wished he could "find a book full of fairytales and love-songs, and not remember anything." He was talking about the curse of the intellect, the weight of constant analysis, and how the remedy might be physical, bodily, almost childlike. Walking is a bit like that. It returns you to simplicity. It empties you. It makes room.

Sometimes I think that our age — the age of screens, of notifications, of endless scrolling — has accidentally discovered the opposite of walking. To walk is to be present, in a place, in a body, moving slowly. To scroll is to be absent, everywhere and nowhere, frozen, flickering. Walking gives you continuity; scrolling gives you fragments. Walking gives you a horizon; scrolling gives you a feed.

I want to be a person who walks. Not because it is healthy, though it is. Not because it is ecological, though it is. But because it is a way of paying attention, a way of saying yes to the world, a way of keeping the mind porous and the heart soft.

There is a line by the poet Wendell Berry: "You do not have to be good. You do not have to walk on your knees for a hundred miles through the desert, repenting." He is quoting Rilke, actually, adapting him. But the line sticks with me: you do not have to walk on your knees. The walking you do on your own two feet, on the humble streets, under the ordinary sky — that is enough. That is already a kind of grace.

So here is what I would say to you, whoever you are, reading this: go for a walk. Not a power walk. Not a hike with a checklist. Just a walk. Leave your phone at home, or put it on silent. Choose a direction based on nothing. Notice the cracks in the sidewalk. Notice the light. Let your mind wander. Don't force it. If you end up solving a problem, fine. If you end up thinking about nothing at all, better. Walk until you forget you're walking. Walk until you remember you're alive.

That's what I want to write about. That's what I'm always trying to get back to.
